title: Stewart v. Rosenblum
description: Whether sections 110-6 and 110-6.1 of the Pretrial Fairness Act violate the separation of powers clause of the Illinois Constitution by unduly infringing on a circuit court judge's inherent authority to detain defendants indefinitely pending trial.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner, Aimee Stewart, argued that her indefinite detention was unlawful because the Pretrial Fairness Act did not provide statutory authority for it, and the judge's declaration of the Act as unconstitutional was premature and incorrect.
defendant_argument: The respondent, Judge Steven J. Rosenblum, argued that the Pretrial Fairness Act was unconstitutional as applied to the petitioner's case because it unduly limited his inherent judicial authority to administer justice and manage his docket, especially when a defendant repeatedly fails to appear in court.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's judgment, finding that the Pretrial Fairness Act is constitutional and does not violate the separation of powers clause, and that the respondent lacked the authority to indefinitely detain the petitioner. The court granted the petitioner's writ of habeas corpus and ordered her immediate release.

title: State v. Spencer
description: Whether Eugene Spencer's 100-year aggregate sentence, imposed when he was 20, violates the Illinois proportionate penalties clause as a de facto life sentence, and whether the youth parole statute cures any unconstitutionality.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Spencer's 100-year sentence is constitutional because his eligibility for parole after 20 years under the youth parole statute prevents it from being a de facto life sentence, thus not violating the proportionate penalties clause.
defendant_argument: Spencer argued that his 100-year sentence is a de facto life sentence without proper consideration of youth-related factors, violating the proportionate penalties clause, and that the parole statute does not provide a meaningful opportunity for parole, thus not curing the unconstitutional sentence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower courts' judgments, finding that Spencer's 100-year sentence was not a de facto life sentence due to parole eligibility, and that Miller v. Alabama does not apply to emerging adults, but clarified that Spencer is not foreclosed from bringing an as-applied challenge in postconviction proceedings.

title: McCombie v. Illinois State Board of Elections
description: Whether the plaintiffs' motion to challenge the 2021 legislative redistricting plan, alleging it violates constitutional requirements for compact districts and political fairness, is timely or barred by the equitable doctrine of laches.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue their motion is timely, relying on federal and out-of-state case law, and that the 2021 Enacted Plan violates the Illinois Constitution by featuring gerrymandered districts for partisan purposes and lacking compactness.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the plaintiffs' motion is untimely and barred by the doctrine of laches because it was filed more than three years and two election cycles after the redistricting map was enacted.
decision_outcome: The court denied the plaintiffs' motion for leave to file a complaint for declaratory judgment and injunctive relief, ruling it was untimely and barred by laches.

title: People v. Hagestedt
description: Whether police officers' actions of using a flashlight and an angled view to peer into a chained and locked, slightly ajar kitchen cabinet during a gas leak investigation constituted an unreasonable warrantless search in violation of the Fourth Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The police officers exceeded the scope of their authorized entry (gas leak investigation) and conducted an unreasonable warrantless search by using a flashlight to peer into a chained and locked cabinet, whose contents were not in plain view, thereby violating his Fourth Amendment rights.
defendant_argument: The officers' actions did not constitute a search because the contents were openly or plainly visible, and the use of a flashlight to illuminate a darkened area does not transform an observation into a search. The defendant also failed to prove a reasonable expectation of privacy.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower courts' judgments, ruling that the trial court erred in denying the defendant's motion to suppress evidence, and vacated the defendant's conviction and sentence.

title: People v. White
description: Whether a defendant who enters a blind guilty plea waives the right to challenge their sentence under the proportionate penalties clause, and whether a 40-year sentence for a 20-year-old constitutes a disproportionate penalty.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioner Sedrick White argued that his blind guilty plea did not waive his right to challenge his 40-year sentence as a de facto life sentence violating the proportionate penalties clause, especially given his youth and rehabilitative potential.
defendant_argument: The State conceded that a blind guilty plea does not waive sentencing errors but argued that White's 40-year sentence was not disproportionate and the circuit court properly considered all factors.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the appellate court, albeit on different grounds, and affirmed the judgment of the circuit court, denying the petitioner's claim.

title: Martin v. Goodrich Corporation
description: Whether section 1(f) of the Workers' Occupational Diseases Act is a statute of repose, and if so, whether the exception in section 1.1 applies prospectively without violating Illinois's due process guarantee, with the plaintiff arguing for its application to allow a civil suit and the defendant arguing against it to maintain exclusivity provisions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that section 1(f) is a statute of repose, and the exception in section 1.1 should apply to her case, allowing her to pursue a civil action for her husband's occupational disease and death.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that section 1(f) is not a statute of repose, thus section 1.1 does not apply, and alternatively, that applying section 1.1 to revive the plaintiff's claim would violate their due process rights by infringing on a vested right to a defense.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that section 1(f) is a statute of repose, section 1.1 applies prospectively under section 4 of the Statute on Statutes, and this prospective application does not violate Illinois's due process guarantee, thereby allowing claims like the plaintiff's to proceed.

title: People v. Clark
description: Whether warrantless arrests based on investigative alerts violate the United States and Illinois Constitutions, and whether the circuit court properly applied juvenile sentencing factors.
plaintiff_argument: Warrantless arrests based on probable cause via investigative alerts are constitutional, and the circuit court adequately considered juvenile sentencing factors.
defendant_argument: Warrantless arrests based on investigative alerts are unconstitutional, and the circuit court failed to properly apply juvenile sentencing factors.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's judgment, upholding the defendant's conviction and sentence, finding that investigative alerts do not violate the constitution and that sentencing factors were considered.

title: Walker v. Chasteen
description: Whether the circuit court has subject-matter jurisdiction to order refunds of unconstitutional filing fees, or if such claims must be brought in the Court of Claims under sovereign immunity principles.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the officer-suit exception to sovereign immunity applies to both their claim for injunctive relief and their claim for refunds, asserting that the refund claim is inextricably tied to the injunctive relief and thus the circuit court should decide both.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the officer-suit exception only applied to the claim for prospective injunctive relief, and once the unconstitutional statutes were enjoined, the refund claim became a present claim against the State for a past wrong, which falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Claims due to sovereign immunity.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the appellate court's judgment and affirmed the circuit court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' refund claim, holding that the circuit court lacked jurisdiction over the refund claim due to sovereign immunity.

title: Arlington Heights Pension Fund v. Pritzker
description: Whether Public Act 101-610, which consolidated local police and firefighter pension funds into statewide funds, violates the pension protection clause or the takings clause of the Illinois Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Act diminishes pension benefits by removing local control over investments and diluting voting power, and constitutes a taking of private property by requiring transfer of assets and imposing transition costs.
defendant_argument: The Act does not diminish constitutionally protected pension benefits, as voting rights and investment control are not protected, nor does it constitute a taking of private property, as plaintiffs only have a right to receive payments, not control assets.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower courts' judgments, ruling that Public Act 101-610 does not violate the pension protection clause or the takings clause of the Illinois Constitution.

title: Caulkins v. Pritzker
description: Whether the Protect Illinois Communities Act, which restricts assault weapons and large capacity magazines, violates the Illinois Constitution's equal protection and special legislation clauses due to its exemptions, and whether the Act was passed in violation of the three-readings requirement.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Act's exemptions for certain professionals and grandfathered individuals deny law-abiding citizens equal protection and constitute special legislation, and that the Act violates the three-readings requirement of the Illinois Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Act's exemptions do not deny equal protection or constitute special legislation because the plaintiffs are not similarly situated to the exempt classes, and that the plaintiffs waived their second amendment and three-readings claims.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's judgment, ruling that the Act's exemptions do not violate equal protection or special legislation, and that the plaintiffs waived their second amendment challenge and were jurisdictionally barred from renewing their three-readings claim.

title: Rowe v. Raoul
description: Whether Public Acts 101-652 and 102-1104 (SAFE-T Act), which abolished monetary bail and revised pretrial release provisions, violate the Illinois Constitution's bail clause, crime victims' rights clause, and separation of powers clause.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Act's pretrial release provisions violated the Illinois Constitution's bail clause, crime victims' rights clause, and separation of powers clause, contending that eliminating monetary bail was an improper constitutional amendment, stripped courts of authority, and prevented the protection of victims' safety.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Act was constitutional, asserting that the bail clause does not mandate monetary bail, the Act's provisions adequately consider crime victims' rights, and the legislature has the authority to regulate the bail system without violating separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's decision, ruling that the Public Acts 101-652 and 102-1104 (SAFE-T Act) are constitutional and do not violate the Illinois Constitution.

title: People v. Mayfield
description: Whether the Illinois Supreme Court's emergency administrative orders, which tolled the speedy-trial statute during COVID-19, violated the separation-of-powers clause of the Illinois Constitution by infringing on the General Assembly's legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the court's administrative orders were a valid exercise of its general administrative and supervisory authority over all state courts, and therefore prevailed over the conflicting speedy-trial statute.
defendant_argument: Gary Mayfield argued that the circuit court's noncompliance with the speedy-trial statute compelled reversal of his conviction because the supreme court's administrative orders violated the Illinois Constitution's separation-of-powers clause.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's conviction, holding that its emergency orders tolling the speedy-trial statute did not violate the separation-of-powers clause.

title: People v. Brown
description: Whether defendant Servetus Brown received ineffective assistance of trial counsel because his attorney agreed to a process where juror challenges were exercised off the record and outside his presence, with the plaintiff arguing counsel was effective and the defendant arguing counsel was ineffective.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (State) argued that the defendant's counsel provided adequate assistance and that the defendant failed to demonstrate prejudice from the jury selection process.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his trial counsel was ineffective for failing to object to the off-the-record sidebar conferences for juror challenges held in his absence, which he claimed violated his constitutional right to be present at a critical stage of trial, and that prejudice should be presumed.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the appellate court, which had affirmed the circuit court's judgment, thereby upholding the defendant's conviction.

title: Illinois Road & Transportation Builders Association v. The County of Cook
description: Whether the 2016 'safe roads amendment' to the Illinois Constitution, which mandates that transportation-related revenues be used only for transportation purposes, applies to revenues generated by home-rule units from transportation-related taxes, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The Amendment applies to all moneys derived from transportation-related taxes, fees, excises, or license taxes, including those collected by home-rule units like Cook County, and thus the County is impermissibly diverting these funds for non-transportation purposes.
defendant_argument: The Amendment applies exclusively to state-imposed tax revenues, not revenues imposed by home-rule authority, and therefore Cook County's spending of transportation-related tax revenues on public safety operations is permissible under its home-rule powers.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' complaint, finding that the plaintiffs have associational standing and that the Cook County Transportation Taxes are subject to the Amendment, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: People v. Moon
description: Whether a criminal defendant's trial before an unsworn jury requires automatic reversal without a showing of prejudice to the defendant.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the defendant forfeited the error by not objecting at trial, and the unsworn jury was harmless error not requiring automatic reversal, as the jury was admonished on legal principles during voir dire.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the failure to administer a trial oath to the jury was a structural error, affecting the fundamental right to an impartial jury, and thus required automatic reversal regardless of prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the appellate and circuit courts' judgments, finding the unsworn jury constituted structural error, and remanded the case for a new trial.

title: International Association of Fire Fighters, Local 50 v. The City of Peoria
description: Whether the City of Peoria, as a home rule unit, can define "catastrophic injury" and "injury" in its local ordinance in a manner inconsistent with the state's Public Safety Employee Benefits Act and prior Illinois Supreme Court interpretations.
plaintiff_argument: The Union argued that the City's ordinance improperly redefined "catastrophic injury" and "injury" in a way that violates the Public Safety Employee Benefits Act and established case law, exceeding its home rule authority.
defendant_argument: The City argued it had home rule authority to define these terms for itself, was not bound by prior judicial interpretations without legislative amendment, and that its ordinance was a proper exercise of its powers.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the lower courts' decisions, ruling that the City's ordinance definitions of "catastrophic injury," "injury," and "gainful work" were inconsistent with the Public Safety Employee Benefits Act and therefore invalid.

title: People v. House
description: Whether Antonio House's mandatory natural life sentence for murders committed at age 19 violates the proportionate penalties clause of the Illinois Constitution, with the petitioner arguing it does based on evolving brain science for young adults, and the State arguing the claim was not properly developed in the trial court.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the appellate court erred by ruling on the as-applied proportionate penalties claim without a sufficiently developed evidentiary record in the trial court, as required by Harris. They also agreed to remand the actual innocence claim for reconsideration.
defendant_argument: House argued that his mandatory natural life sentence was unconstitutional as applied to him under the proportionate penalties clause, contending that the reasoning of Miller v. Alabama should extend to young adults aged 18-21 due to scientific evidence on brain development. He also sought cross-relief on his actual innocence claim.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the appellate court's finding that the petitioner's sentence violated the proportionate penalties clause and vacated the appellate court's dismissal of the actual innocence claim, remanding both issues to the circuit court for further second-stage postconviction proceedings to allow for proper record development.

title: People v. McCavitt
description: Whether the Fourth Amendment required police to obtain a new warrant before searching a defendant's computer data for evidence of another crime after his acquittal for a sexual assault, with the plaintiff arguing that the original warrant and plain view doctrine made the search lawful, and the defendant arguing that his expectation of privacy was restored upon acquittal, requiring a new warrant.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the post-acquittal computer examination was a permissible "second look" under the original lawful search warrant, which was broadly written and unchallenged, and that the child pornography found was admissible under the plain view doctrine, thus not violating Fourth Amendment rights.
defendant_argument: McCavitt argued that the search violated his Fourth Amendment rights and expectation of privacy, which was fully restored upon his acquittal for sexual assault, and that law enforcement was required to obtain a new warrant before searching his computer data for evidence of another crime.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the appellate court's judgment and affirmed the trial court's denial of the defendant's motion to suppress the digital images, thereby upholding his convictions for child pornography.

title: Guns Save Life, Inc. v. Ali
description: Whether Cook County's special taxes on the retail purchase of firearms and ammunition violate the uniformity clause of the Illinois Constitution by burdening the fundamental right to bear arms.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the firearm and ammunition taxes violate the Second Amendment, the Illinois Constitution's right to bear arms and uniformity clause, and are preempted by state law, specifically contending that the taxes burden a fundamental right and are not sufficiently related to their stated public safety objective.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the taxes were a proper exercise of Cook County's home rule taxing powers, did not meaningfully impede the right to bear arms, and were substantially related to the important governmental interest of public safety by funding programs to combat gun violence.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the appellate court's judgment, holding that the firearm and ammunition tax ordinances are unconstitutional under the uniformity clause of the Illinois Constitution because they burden a fundamental right without a sufficient relationship between the tax classification and its stated objective.

title: People v. Bochenek
description: Whether the statutory venue provision for identity theft, which allows for proper venue in the county where the victim resides, is constitutional under Article I, Section 8 of the Illinois Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that the venue provision is constitutional because the offense of identity theft can be deemed to have occurred where the victim resides, as the intangible identifying information is 'located' there, and the General Assembly has the authority to define where a crime is committed.
defendant_argument: Bochenek argued that the venue provision is unconstitutional because no aspect of identity theft is connected to the victim's residence, and the offense only occurs where the physical acts were committed.
decision_outcome: The court held that the venue provision for identity theft is constitutional and affirmed the appellate court's judgment, which denied the defendant's motion to dismiss the indictment.

title: People v. Bass
description: Whether a routine traffic stop was unlawfully prolonged by running a name check on a passenger, violating the Fourth Amendment, and whether arrests based on investigative alerts, even with probable cause, violate the Illinois Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued the traffic stop was lawfully executed and not unlawfully prolonged, and that investigative alerts are constitutional under both the United States and Illinois Constitutions.
defendant_argument: Bass argued the traffic stop was unlawfully extended by running a name check unrelated to the red light violation, and that investigative alerts are unconstitutional under Article I, Section 6 of the Illinois Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's decision to reverse Bass's conviction and remand for a new trial due to an unlawfully prolonged traffic stop, but vacated the appellate court's portions dealing with limited lockstep analysis and investigatory alerts.
